opts: It makes state async in a dangerous way

try.task: Write Profile({ onRender }): calls onRender() on every render; a "Load" button sets three pieces of state (name "Ada", age 36, status "ready") from inside a setTimeout. Show name (age) – status. With automatic batching, Load must cause exactly one extra render.
examples: after Load: "Ada (36) – ready" with 1 extra render
try.hint: Three useState calls; in the timeout call all three setters. React 18+ batches them.

tests.code:
import { render, screen, fireEvent, act } from '@testing-library/react'
import { afterEach, beforeEach, expect, test, vi } from 'vitest'
import { Profile } from './Profile'

beforeEach(() => vi.useFakeTimers())
afterEach(() => vi.useRealTimers())

test('initial state', () => {
  render(<Profile />)
  expect(screen.getByText('(0) – idle', { exact: false })).toBeTruthy()
})

test('loads all three values', () => {
  render(<Profile />)
  fireEvent.click(screen.getByText('Load'))
  act(() => vi.runAllTimers())
  expect(screen.getByText('Ada (36) – ready')).toBeTruthy()
})

test('three updates in a timeout cause one render', () => {
  let renders = 0
  render(<Profile onRender={() => renders++} />)
  const before = renders
  fireEvent.click(screen.getByText('Load'))
  act(() => vi.runAllTimers())
  expect(renders - before).toBe(1)
})

checks.t: three updates in a timeout cause one render

takeaway.key: React 18+ batches all updates in the same tick into one render, everywhere. flushSync forces an immediate render when you must read the DOM.

think.q: Why did React switch from recursive rendering (stack reconciler) to fibers?

why: A recursive call stack cannot be paused halfway.

think.q: Where does a component's useState value live?

On its fiber, in a linked list of hooks (memoizedState)
why: That list is why hook order matters.

opts: The tree on screen, and the one being built for the next commit; they swap at commit
Old and new versions of React
why: The work-in-progress tree can be discarded without touching the screen.

why: That is the whole traversal: child → sibling → return.

dryRun.title: workLoop with a 5 ms budget per slice
rows: time is up → yield to the browser
dryRun.note: In concurrent rendering React processes fibers in a loop and checks shouldYield() between units. When the slice (about 5 ms) is used up it gives control back so input and painting stay smooth, then continues. Only the commit is done in one go.

think.q: What does "yielding" mean in the work loop?
opts: Stopping after a unit of work so the browser can handle input and paint, then resuming later
why: That is what keeps typing responsive during a big render.

think.q: Can the commit phase be split across frames like rendering?
opts: No, the commit is synchronous so users never see a half-updated UI
why: Only render is interruptible.

think.q: Which updates use the time-sliced, interruptible loop?
opts: Transitions and other concurrent updates (startTransition, useDeferredValue)
why: Urgent updates like typing still render synchronously.

think.q: What stops a low-priority render from being postponed forever?
opts: Lanes have expiration: work that waits too long is treated as urgent
why: Starvation protection is part of the scheduler.

think.q: Which browser API does a similar "do work while idle" job?
why: React ships its own scheduler (MessageChannel-based) because rIC is not reliable enough.

try.task: Write a time-sliced runner: createWorkLoop(units, { budget, now }) returns { runSlice() }. Each runSlice processes units (functions) until the budget (ms, measured with the injected now()) is used, and returns { done, processed } for that slice.
examples: const loop = createWorkLoop(tasks, { budget: 5, now: fakeClock })
try.hint: In runSlice: const start = now(); while (i < units.length && now() - start < budget) { units[i++]() }.

checks.t: stops when the budget is used
continues where it stopped, in order
always makes progress even if one unit is slow

takeaway.key: Concurrent rendering processes fibers in short slices and yields to the browser between them; the commit stays synchronous.
mistakes: Expecting every update to be interruptible.
Long synchronous work inside one component (it cannot be sliced).

dryRun.title: Updates in the same moment
rows: when urgent work is done; can be interrupted
dryRun.note: React gives every update a lane (a priority bit). Urgent lanes render first; transition lanes can be interrupted and restarted when something urgent arrives. The scheduler package orders the work using a priority queue.

opts: The keystroke renders first; the list render is interrupted and restarted with the new input
The keystroke waits for the list
Both render at the same time
The list render is lost forever
why: That is the point of marking non-urgent updates.

think.q: Why bitmask "lanes" instead of one number?
opts: Several priorities can be pending and batched together, checked with fast bit operations
why: A render can handle a set of lanes at once.

opts: Mark non-urgent updates with startTransition / useTransition / useDeferredValue
why: React assigns lanes from how the update was triggered.

try.task: Write a tiny priority scheduler: createScheduler() with schedule(name, priority) (lower number = more urgent) and flush() returning task names in run order: by priority, then first-scheduled first.
